Experts think there will soon be more oil than people want to buy. When there is a lot of something, it usually gets cheaper. A report said the US also has plenty of oil stored, which helped the price go down.
A war involving Iran has made things harder. Ships have trouble using a key sea road. When oil costs more, petrol and heating cost more too. That can make prices in shops go up, because lorries need petrol.
levels.why: When oil is cheaper, petrol and heating can cost less.

levels.headline: Oil is getting cheaper, but it still costs a lot
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid from under the ground. We use it to make petrol for cars and buses. On 17 November, one big barrel of oil cost about $92. That is cheaper than last month. But it still costs more than it did a year ago.
Experts think there will soon be a lot of oil to buy. When there is plenty of something, it tends to cost less. A report said America has lots of oil in storage, which also helps prices fall.
A war involving Iran has made oil harder to move by ship. When oil costs more, petrol costs more too. That can make shop prices go up, because lorries use petrol to bring food to shops.
levels.why: Cheaper oil can mean cheaper petrol and food.

levels.headline: Oil is getting a little cheaper
levels.body:
Oil is a thick black liquid from deep under the ground. People use it to make petrol for cars. Its price goes up and down, like the price of sweets at different shops. This week, the price of a big barrel of oil fell to about $92. That is cheaper than last month.
It is still more expensive than a year ago, though. Experts think there will soon be a lot of oil to buy. When there is lots of something, it often gets cheaper. America also has lots of oil stored away.
A war involving Iran has made it harder for ships to carry oil. When oil costs more, petrol costs more, and so can food, because lorries need petrol to bring it to shops. So cheaper oil can help families a little.
levels.why: Cheaper oil can help families spend less on petrol and food.

headline: EU forecasts eurozone growth of 1.2% this year and next, but warns the energy shock will keep inflation above 3%

terms.meaning: The 21 EU countries that use the euro, or the group of countries using it.
How much a country's total output of goods and services grows.
An expert estimate of what will happen in future.

levels.headline: EU forecasts eurozone growth of 1.2% this year and next, but warns the energy shock will keep inflation above 3%
levels.body:
The European Commission's autumn 2026 economic forecast, published on 17 November, put eurozone growth at 1.2% for both this year and next. That is up from the 0.9% it expected for 2026 in the spring, when it had cut its outlook because of the Strait of Hormuz crisis.
The Commission said inflation will stay above 3% this year and next as the Iran war keeps energy prices high. Among the four biggest eurozone economies, Spain is forecast to grow fastest at 2.6%, ahead of Germany at 1.3% and Italy at 1.0%. France lags at 0.4%.
EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis warned France to rein in its debt even as the growth outlook improves. For the UK, the eurozone is the biggest trading partner, so its growth and inflation affect British exporters and prices, as well as the Bank of England's choices.
levels.why: Europe is Britain's biggest trading partner, so its growth affects UK jobs and exports.

levels.headline: EU upgrades eurozone growth forecast to 1.2% but says inflation will stay above 3%
levels.body:
The European Commission published its autumn economic forecast on 17 November, projecting eurozone growth of 1.2% this year and next. In spring it had expected only 0.9% for 2026 after the Strait of Hormuz crisis pushed up energy costs.
The Commission still expects inflation above 3% in both years because the Iran war keeps energy prices high. Spain is expected to grow fastest among the big four at 2.6%, followed by Germany at 1.3% and Italy at 1.0%. France is forecast to grow just 0.4%.
Valdis Dombrovskis, the EU economy commissioner, warned France to bring its debt under control. The eurozone is the UK's biggest trading partner, so its performance matters for British businesses.
levels.why: What happens to European growth and prices affects UK exports and costs.

levels.headline: EU raises eurozone growth forecast to 1.2% while warning of higher inflation
levels.body:
The European Commission has raised its growth forecast for the eurozone to 1.2% for this year and next, up from 0.9% expected for 2026 in the spring. The autumn forecast was published on 17 November.
However, the Commission said inflation will stay above 3% in both years as the war involving Iran keeps energy prices high. Spain is forecast to grow fastest of the four biggest economies, at 2.6%, with Germany at 1.3%, Italy at 1.0% and France at just 0.4%.
EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis told France to rein in its debt. Because the eurozone is the UK's largest trading partner, its prospects matter to British firms and to prices here.
levels.why: It matters to UK trade and to prices in the shops.

levels.headline: The EU says its economy is doing better than expected, but prices will stay high
levels.body:
The European Commission, the EU's executive body, says the economy of the eurozone is doing better than it feared. On 17 November it said it expects the economy to grow by 1.2% this year and next. In the spring it had expected 0.9% for this year.
But prices are still rising fast. The Commission expects inflation to stay above 3% this year and next, because energy costs more after the war involving Iran. Spain should grow the fastest of the biggest countries, at 2.6%. Germany should grow by 1.3%, Italy by 1.0% and France by only 0.4%.
The EU's economy chief, Valdis Dombrovskis, told France to bring down its debts. The eurozone is Britain's biggest trading partner, so its health matters to British businesses.
levels.why: A stronger Europe is good for UK firms that sell there.

levels.headline: The EU says its economy is doing a bit better, but prices will stay high
levels.body:
The European Commission is the EU's main decision-making body. On 17 November it said the economy of the countries that use the euro should grow by 1.2% this year and next. That is better than the 0.9% it expected in the spring.
But prices are still going up fast. It thinks inflation, meaning how fast prices rise, will stay above 3% for two years. Energy costs a lot because of the war involving Iran. Spain should grow fastest of the big four at 2.6%. Germany should grow by 1.3%, Italy by 1.0% and France by only 0.4%.
The EU's economy chief told France to bring down its debts. Countries that use the euro are Britain's biggest trading partners, so their health matters to British firms.
levels.why: UK firms sell a lot to Europe, so its growth helps them.

levels.headline: The EU says its economy will grow a little, but prices will stay high
levels.body:
The EU is a group of European countries. Many of them use the same money, the euro. Experts at the EU said on 17 November that these countries' economies should grow by about 1.2% this year and next. That is a bit better than they thought earlier in the year.
But prices are still rising quickly. The experts think prices will keep going up by more than 3% a year for two years. Energy costs a lot because of the war involving Iran. Spain should do best of the big four countries, and France should do worst.
This matters to Britain because countries that use the euro buy a lot of what we make. If they do well, British firms can sell more. If prices stay high there, the cost of things from Europe may stay high too.
levels.why: Our biggest customers are in Europe, so how they do affects British jobs.

levels.headline: The EU says its countries will grow a little, but prices will stay high
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe are part of the EU. Lots of them use the same money, called the euro. On 17 November, EU experts said these countries' economies should grow by about 1.2% a year for the next two years. That is a bit better than they expected before.
But prices will keep rising fast. They think prices will go up by more than 3% a year for two years. Energy costs a lot because of a war involving Iran. Spain should do best out of the four biggest countries. France should do worst.
This matters to Britain. Countries in Europe buy a lot of things we make and sell. If they do well, British firms can sell more. If they are struggling, our firms may sell less.
levels.why: Europe buys lots of British goods, so its growth matters here.

levels.headline: Europe's economy will grow a little, but prices stay high
levels.body:
Europe has lots of countries. Many of them share the same money, called the euro. Experts looked at how their money-making will go. A country's economy is all the things people make, sell and buy. They said it should grow by a small amount, about 1.2%, each year for two years.
That is a bit better than they thought before. But prices are still going up fast. Things like petrol and gas cost more because of a war involving Iran. The experts said prices will go up by more than 3% a year.
This matters to Britain because Europe is our nearest neighbour and a very big customer. If Europe does well, British shops and factories can sell more there.
levels.why: Britain sells lots to Europe, so how Europe does matters here.

levels.headline: Europe's money-making is growing a little
levels.body:
Europe is full of countries that sell things to each other. All the things they make, sell and buy are called the economy. Experts said on 17 November that this economy should grow a little, by about 1.2% each year for two years. That is slightly better than they thought.
But prices are still rising. Petrol and gas cost more because of a war involving Iran. The experts say prices will keep going up by more than 3% a year. That means things in shops cost a bit more each year.
This matters to Britain because Europe is our nearest neighbour. We sell lots of things there. If Europe does well, our shops and factories can sell more to them.
levels.why: Britain sells lots of things to Europe.

levels.headline: Europe's money-making is growing a tiny bit
levels.body:
Think of Europe as a big neighbourhood where countries buy and sell things from each other. Experts said this week that the neighbourhood is growing a tiny bit richer. They think it will grow by a small amount, about 1 in every 100, each year for two years. That is a bit better than they thought before.
But prices are still going up. Things like petrol and gas cost more because of a war far away. That means a toy or a loaf of bread can cost more than it did last year. The experts think prices will keep going up for a while.
This matters to Britain, because Europe is our nearest neighbour. We sell lots of things there, and buy lots from there.
levels.why: Europe is Britain's nearest neighbour and a big customer.

headline: Serbia's Student List wins outright majority as Vucic concedes after nearly two years of protests

terms.meaning: An election called earlier than normally scheduled.
A politician who claims to speak for ordinary people against the elite.
More than half of the seats in a parliament.

levels.headline: Serbia's Student List wins outright majority as Vucic concedes after nearly two years of protests
levels.body:
The student-backed Student List won Serbia's snap parliamentary election on 25 October, taking 140 of the 250 seats for an outright majority, according to projections reported by Euronews and CNBC. The count was not yet final. Long-time populist leader Aleksandar Vucic conceded on election night.
Mr Vucic had resigned as president on 27 September to run for prime minister, after nearly two years of student-led protests. His SNS party was projected to win about 105 seats. He blamed independent media, alleged interference by unnamed European countries and an American deep state for the defeat.
None of the student organisers stood on the list. Its candidates were little-known experts, athletes, farmers and artists. The EU welcomed the result, though analysts say the new government must show it can govern, and its stance on Russia sanctions and Kosovo is unclear. Euronews reported on 17 November that the students have now entered parliament.
levels.why: It is one of the biggest political shifts in the Balkans in years and could reshape Serbia's ties with the EU and Russia.

levels.headline: Serbia's students win election as Vucic admits defeat
levels.body:
The Student List, a movement born from nearly two years of student-led protests, won Serbia's snap election on 25 October. Projections gave it 140 of the 250 seats in parliament, an outright majority, although the count was not final. President-turned-candidate Aleksandar Vucic conceded on election night.
Mr Vucic had resigned as president on 27 September to stand for prime minister. His SNS party was projected to win around 105 seats. He blamed Serbia's independent media, alleged interference by unnamed European countries and an American deep state.
No student leaders were on the list, which was made up of little-known experts, athletes, farmers and artists. EU leaders welcomed the result. Analysts say the new government still has to prove it can govern, and its position on Russia sanctions and Kosovo is unclear.
levels.why: Serbia's direction towards the EU or Russia may change.

levels.headline: Student-backed list wins Serbia's election as Vucic concedes
levels.body:
A student-backed movement has won the Serbian parliamentary election held on 25 October. The Student List took about 140 of the 250 seats, enough for a majority, according to projections reported by Euronews and CNBC. The count was not yet final.
Aleksandar Vucic, who resigned as president on 27 September to run for prime minister, conceded on election night. His SNS party was projected to take about 105 seats. He blamed independent media, alleged interference by European countries and an American deep state.
The list had no student leaders on it. Its candidates were mostly little-known experts, athletes, farmers and artists. The EU welcomed the outcome. Analysts say the new government must show it can run the country, and its views on Russia sanctions and Kosovo are unknown.
levels.why: The result could change Serbia's relations with the EU and Russia.

levels.headline: Students win Serbia's election after months of protests
levels.body:
A movement led by students has won an election in Serbia. The vote, held on 25 October, was held earlier than planned. Projections said the Student List won 140 of the 250 seats in parliament, which is more than half. The final count was not yet finished.
Serbia's long-time leader, Aleksandar Vucic, accepted defeat on election night. He had left his job as president on 27 September so he could run to be prime minister. His party was expected to win about 105 seats. He blamed the media and unnamed foreign interference.
The students themselves did not stand. The list was made up of little-known experts, athletes, farmers and artists. EU leaders welcomed the result. Experts say the new government will have to show it can run the country.
levels.why: Serbia's future ties with the EU and Russia could change.

levels.headline: Students win Serbia's election after long protests
levels.body:
Serbia is a country in south-east Europe. For almost two years, students there held protests against the government. Now a group backed by the students has won an election. The vote was on 25 October. They won 140 of the 250 seats in parliament, which is more than half.
The country's leader for many years, Aleksandar Vucic, said he had lost. He had stepped down as president so he could try to become prime minister. His party won about 105 seats. He blamed the media and foreign countries, but gave no proof.
The students did not put their own leaders on the list. It was made of experts, athletes, farmers and artists. The EU welcomed the result. Now the new group has to show it can run the country.
levels.why: It could change how close Serbia gets to the EU or to Russia.

levels.headline: Students win an election in Serbia
levels.body:
Serbia is a country in Europe. For almost two years, students there held big protests against the government. On 25 October, people voted in an election, and a group backed by the students won. They got 140 of the 250 seats in parliament, which is more than half.
The leader for many years, Aleksandar Vucic, said he had lost. He had left his job as president to try to become prime minister. His party won about 105 seats. He blamed the media and other countries.
The students did not choose their own leaders to stand. The group chose experts, athletes, farmers and artists instead. The EU said it was pleased. Now the new group has to show it can run the country well.
levels.why: Serbia could become closer to the EU.

levels.headline: Students win an election and change who runs Serbia
levels.body:
Serbia is a country in Europe. For almost two years, students held big protests there because they were unhappy with the government. On 25 October, people voted in an election. The group backed by the students won, which was a big surprise.
They got 140 of the 250 places in parliament, which is more than half. That means they can make decisions. The country's leader for many years, Aleksandar Vucic, said he had lost.
The group did not choose student leaders to stand. It chose experts, athletes, farmers and artists. Countries in the EU were pleased. Now the new group has to show it can run the country well.
levels.why: People who protested peacefully have changed who runs their country.

levels.headline: Students win an election in Serbia
levels.body:
Serbia is a country in Europe. Students there were upset with the people who ran the country. For almost two years, they held big protests. On 25 October, everyone was asked to vote. The group the students backed won, which surprised many people.
The group won more than half of the places in parliament. Parliament is where people meet to make the rules. The man who had been in charge for many years, Aleksandar Vucic, said he had lost.
The students did not pick student leaders. They picked experts, athletes, farmers and artists. Other countries in Europe said they were pleased. Now the winners have to show they can run Serbia well.
levels.why: Voting can change who is in charge.

levels.headline: Students win an election in Serbia
levels.body:
Serbia is a country in Europe. The students there were unhappy with how it was run. They marched and protested for almost two years. Then everybody was asked to vote, and the group the students backed won.
It won more than half the places in parliament. Parliament is a big room where grown-ups meet to make the rules. The man who had been in charge for a long time said he had lost.
The students did not choose their own leaders. They chose people like farmers, artists and athletes. Other countries in Europe said that was good news. Now the winners have to show they can do a good job.
levels.why: Voting can change who is in charge.

levels.headline: Students win an election in a faraway country
levels.body:
Serbia is a country in Europe. Students there were not happy with the way it was run. For nearly two years they marched and held signs. Then the whole country voted, a bit like choosing a class captain, and the group the students backed won.
The group won more than half of the places in a big meeting room called parliament. That is where grown-ups make the rules. The man who had been in charge for a long time said he had lost.
The group chose farmers, artists and athletes to stand, not just the students. Now they have to prove they can do a good job, like a new class captain on their first day.
levels.why: A vote can change who is in charge.

headline: UK to send more than 1,000 air defence missiles to Ukraine and deliver £240 million in winter support

terms.meaning: Weapons and systems that protect against attack from the sky, such as missiles and drones.
Aid to keep Ukrainians safe and warm in winter, including energy supplies.
The government's annual plan for taxes and spending.

levels.headline: UK to send more than 1,000 air defence missiles to Ukraine and deliver £240 million in winter support
levels.body:
The Ministry of Defence announced on 17 November that the UK will provide more than 1,000 air defence missiles to Ukraine, alongside £240 million in winter support. The government said the package forms part of the £500 million announced at the Budget.
The announcement was made by the Ministry of Defence, whose release names Wes Streeting as Defence Secretary. It comes as Russia and Ukraine continue to trade strikes, including Ukraine's attack on the Kerch Bridge, and as European countries debate how to support Kyiv and their place in any peace talks.
Elsewhere, Germany and Norway have said they plan to buy more US air defences for Ukraine. Air defence weapons are used to shoot down drones and missiles aimed at Ukrainian cities and energy sites, and winter support helps keep power and heating running.
levels.why: It shows how the UK is backing Ukraine as winter nears and peace talks begin.

levels.headline: UK announces more than 1,000 air defence missiles and £240m of winter help for Ukraine
levels.body:
The UK government announced on 17 November that it will send more than 1,000 air defence missiles to Ukraine and provide £240 million in winter support. The Ministry of Defence says this is part of the £500 million set out at the Budget.
The release names Wes Streeting as Defence Secretary. The announcement comes as fighting continues and as European countries discuss how to back Ukraine and its role in peace talks. Germany and Norway have said they plan to buy more US air defences for Kyiv.
Air defence missiles are used to shoot down attacking drones and missiles, while winter support is meant to help keep homes powered and heated when it is cold.
levels.why: It signals continued UK military and humanitarian support for Ukraine.

levels.headline: UK to give Ukraine more than 1,000 air defence missiles and £240m for winter
levels.body:
The UK will send Ukraine more than 1,000 air defence missiles and provide £240 million to help it through winter, the Ministry of Defence announced on 17 November. The government says the package is part of the £500 million announced at the Budget.
The announcement names Wes Streeting as Defence Secretary. It follows new talks between Ukrainian, US and European negotiators about starting peace negotiations, and further Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets. Germany and Norway also plan to buy more US air defences for Ukraine.
Air defence missiles protect cities and energy sites from drones and missiles. Winter support helps keep power and heating going when temperatures drop.
levels.why: It shows how much the UK is committing as the war and winter continue.

levels.headline: Britain will send Ukraine more than 1,000 missiles to defend against air attacks
levels.body:
The British government has said it will send Ukraine more than 1,000 air defence missiles. It will also give £240 million to help Ukraine through the winter. The Ministry of Defence announced the plan on 17 November. It says it is part of £500 million promised at the Budget.
The release names Wes Streeting as the Defence Secretary. The announcement comes while talks about peace have only just started and fighting goes on. Germany and Norway also plan to buy more air defences from the US for Ukraine.
Air defence missiles are used to shoot down drones and other missiles before they hit buildings. The winter money is meant to help keep the lights on and homes warm.
levels.why: It shows the UK is still backing Ukraine as the cold weather arrives.

levels.headline: Britain will send Ukraine more than 1,000 missiles to defend against air attacks
levels.body:
The UK government says it will send Ukraine more than 1,000 missiles to help it defend against attacks from the air. It will also give £240 million to help people in Ukraine through the winter. The announcement was made on 17 November. It is part of £500 million promised at the Budget.
Air defence missiles are weapons that shoot down drones and other missiles before they hit buildings. Ukraine's cities and power stations have been attacked from the air. Germany and Norway also plan to buy more air defences for Ukraine.
The winter money is meant to help keep the electricity on and homes warm when it gets very cold. Peace talks have started, but the fighting has not stopped.
levels.why: It helps protect people and keep them warm in winter.

levels.headline: Britain is sending Ukraine more missiles to protect it from air attacks
levels.body:
The UK government says it will send more than 1,000 missiles to Ukraine. These missiles are used to shoot down things that fly towards buildings, like drones and other missiles. The UK will also give £240 million to help people in Ukraine through the winter.
The announcement was made on 17 November. The money is part of £500 million that the government promised at the Budget, which is when it sets out its plans for taxes and spending. Germany and Norway are also planning to buy more air defences for Ukraine.
Winter in Ukraine is very cold. The money should help keep power on and homes warm. Talks about peace have started, but the fighting has not stopped yet.
levels.why: It protects people in Ukraine and shows where UK money is going.

levels.headline: Britain is sending Ukraine missiles and money for the winter
levels.body:
Ukraine is in a war with Russia. Aeroplanes without pilots, called drones, and missiles are sent to hit its cities. To protect them, Ukraine uses special missiles that shoot these things down. On 17 November, Britain said it will send more than 1,000 of these missiles.
Britain will also give £240 million to help people in Ukraine get through winter. Winter there is very cold. The money should help keep power stations working and homes warm. It is part of £500 million that the government promised earlier.
Some other countries, like Germany and Norway, are also planning to help with more defences. People have started to talk about how to make peace, but the war has not stopped.
levels.why: It helps keep people safe and warm.

levels.headline: Britain is sending missiles and money to help Ukraine
levels.body:
Ukraine is in a war with Russia. Flying machines and missiles are sent to hit its towns. Ukraine needs special missiles to shoot them down before they land. On 17 November, Britain said it will send more than 1,000 of these.
Britain will also give a lot of money, £240 million, to help people in Ukraine get through winter. It is very cold there. The money should help keep the lights on and homes warm. It is part of a larger amount the government promised before.
Other countries, like Germany and Norway, are also helping. People have begun to talk about how to make peace, but the war has not stopped yet.
levels.why: It helps keep people safe and warm.

levels.headline: Britain is sending help to a country in a war
levels.body:
Ukraine is a country in Europe that is fighting a war. Its towns are sometimes hit by missiles and flying machines. To keep people safe, Ukraine uses special missiles that shoot these things down. Britain said it will send more than 1,000 of them.
Britain will also send money to help people stay warm in winter. It gets very cold in Ukraine. The money helps keep the lights on and the heating working in people's homes.
Other countries are helping too. Some grown-ups have started to talk about how to make peace. But the war has not stopped yet, so people still need help.
levels.why: Britain is helping people stay safe and warm.

levels.headline: Britain sends help to a country that is in a war
levels.body:
Ukraine is a country that is in a war. Sometimes missiles and flying machines are sent to hit its towns. Ukraine uses special missiles to catch them in the sky, a bit like catching a ball before it hits the window. Britain said it will send more than 1,000 of them.
Britain will also send money so that people in Ukraine can stay warm in winter. It gets very, very cold there. The money helps keep the lights on and the heating working in people's homes.
Other countries are helping too. Grown-ups have started to talk about how to make peace. But the war has not stopped yet.
levels.why: Helping others stay safe and warm is a kind thing to do.
